newsitem.title: UK: Euromarket looks to London as 21st century base.
newsitem.headline: Euromarket looks to London as 21st century base.

text.p: London, home to the expanding Eurobond market, has little to fear from other European centres as it moves into the next millenium and faces the challenges of a single European currency, bankers said.
The belief was reinforced on Tuesday when Dresdner Bank AG said it would base its Eurobond operations in London, following similar moves by other top German banks.

"These days borrowers want to talk different structures, currencies, markets. You've got to have your sales and trading desks and syndicate department all under the one roof if you want to compete in the future," said Tim Skeet, executive director debt capital markets at Lehman Brothers International.
Nearly $550 billion of Eurobonds have been launched already this year, after a record-breaking $464 billion in 1995.

Dresdner Bank, Germany's second largest commercial bank, said it was buying a boutique Eurobond firm, Luthy Baillie Dowsett & Pethick, in conjunction with moving its Eurobond operations from Frankfurt to London.

Responsibility for Dresdner's German government and domestic bond operations will remain in Frankfurt. The Bundesbank requires German banks to maintain a real, tangible syndicate infrastructure in Germany.
The free-wheeling Eurobond market has always favoured the less stringently regulated regime in London.
So even if Britain does not join a single European currency group in 1999 -- as many suspect will be the case -- the Euromarket still expects to treat London as its home base.
The Euromarket's first deals were launched as investments for dollar deposit holders who, for one reason or another, did not want their money held in the U.S.
London, by far the main European financial centre then, attracted that early business and easily managed to hold onto it as the Eurobond market took off in the late 1970s.
Deals continued to be almost exclusively issued out of London during the 1980s. The dollar was the dominant currency.
"The mark was only a small sub-section of the market then. Nobody was interested in it," said Skeet at Lehman Brothers.
By the late 1980s mark and French franc issuance began to pick up and Frankfurt and Paris started to get some of the business.

In the case of Paris, this was partially cosmetic. In many instances, London branches of French banks actually did all the paper work while the Paris headquarters got the credit in the industry league tables.
The dollar is less dominant now but still accounts for about 40 percent of total volume in the international bond markets, according to figures from Capital DATA Bondware.
In the first nine months of the year it accounted for deals worth $208 billion out of a total $509 billion.
Dresdner lead managed 41 deals worth the equivalent of $9.3 billion in the same period, making it 19th in the league table.
"It's playing catch-up," said one new issues trader at a U.S. Bank in London, noting Deutsche Bank and Commerzbank have both recently beefed up their London Eurobond operations.
"The Germans are massive borrowers. But it's only in the past four or five years they have gone international in a big way as we've begun to see a significant offshore bid," he said.
